extraction.name: FOMO60K
extraction.description: A large-scale, heterogeneous dataset of 60,529 brain MRI scans from 13,900 sessions and 11,187 subjects, aggregated from 16 publicly available sources. The dataset includes both clinical- and research-grade images, multiple MRI sequences, and a wide range of anatomical and pathological variability, including scans with large brain anomalies.
extraction.creator: Asbjørn Munk, Stefano Cerri, Jakob Ambsdorf, Julia Machnio, Sebastian Nørgaard Llambias, Vardan Nersesjan, Christian Hedeager Krag, Peirong Liu, Pablo Rocamora García, Mostafa Mehdipour Ghazi, Mikael Boesen, Michael Eriksen Benros, Juan Eugenio Iglesias, and Mads Nielsen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: FOMO60K is a large-scale dataset aggregated from 16 publicly available neuroimaging sources, comprising 60,529 brain MRI scans from 13,900 sessions and 11,187 subjects. The dataset spans both clinical- and research-grade imaging, includes multiple MRI sequences (T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI, and others), and captures anatomical and pathological diversity including scans with large brain anomalies. Minimal preprocessing was applied to retain raw characteristics while improving usability.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of brain MRI scans from 16 publicly available datasets with multiple sequence types including T1-weighted (T1), T2-weighted (T2), Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR), Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI), contrast-enhanced T1 (T1ce), Proton Density (PD), Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI), and Gradient Echo (GRE). Most datasets include at least T1-weighted scans.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Existing resources such as ADNI, UK Biobank, PPMI, and ABCD, while valuable, are often curated for specific diseases or patient populations, and typically follow homogeneous imaging protocols with limited pathological variability. Access is often restricted by formal applications, data use agreements, and institutional approvals, and data are commonly distributed in formats that require domain-specific preprocessing.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: To protect privacy and prevent easy identification of dataset sources, subjects have been shuffled. Skull-stripping was only applied when the images were not already defaced or skull-stripped by the dataset provider, or when visual inspection identified residual cranial features that could compromise anonymization.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: FOMO60K is intended to support the development and benchmarking of self-supervised learning methods in medical imaging at scale. The dataset can be used with no further pre-processing for pre-training. Code for self-supervised pretraining and fine-tuning is provided to facilitate benchmarking, method development, and broader adoption of SSL in medical imaging.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset will continue to grow in future releases as additional cohorts and modalities become available.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) scans stored in 4D format, if a b=0 (non-diffusion-weighted) volume was available, it was extracted and saved separately. For the b=1000 shell, three diffusion-weighted volumes were selected based on their gradient directions being most closely aligned with the canonical x, y, and z axes. The corresponding volumes were averaged to produce a single representative 3D image. To protect privacy and prevent easy identification of dataset sources, subjects have been shuffled.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: MRI preprocessing comprised three main steps: reorienting images to RAS (Right–Anterior–Superior) orientation, affine co-registration, and skull-stripping. All scans were first reoriented to RAS and affinely co-registered using the mri_coreg command from FreeSurfer 7.4.1, with default parameters. Within each MRI session, scans were aligned to the image with the highest spatial resolution to preserve anatomical detail. Skull-stripping was performed using SynthSeg (FreeSurfer 7.4.1), which outputs segmentation masks of brain structures. These masks were used to define the brain extraction region. Skull-stripping was only applied when the images were not already defaced or skull-stripped by the dataset provider, or when visual inspection identified residual cranial features that could compromise anonymization.
